newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel calls for NATO expansion timetable.
newsitem.headline: Havel calls for NATO expansion timetable.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel called on NATO leaders on Saturday to lay out a clear timetable for expansion after the first wave of former-Communist countries are invited to join at a summit next month in Madrid.

Opening a NATO security forum with a dinner speech to ministers, diplomats and top military officials, Havel -- whose country is a frontrunner for membership -- said aspirants not invited should know why and what comes next.

"I think it would be excellent...that at the Madrid summit there would be some logic of expansion laid out, and some schedule indicated with an explanation of why or not some countries were taken earlier and whether or not they may be accepted later," Havel said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton announced last week that Washington's "firm" position was that only Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic should be invited into NATO's first round of expansion into former Communist Eastern Europe.
Havel said it was unrealistic to include all aspirants at once, but those not invited needed hope for what lies ahead.
NATO leaders meet in Madrid July 8-9 and the United States has set 1999, the alliance's 50th anniversary, as the target date for admission for the first wave of aspirants.

Romania and Slovenia -- with France and Italy respectively pushing their inclusion in Madrid -- are hoping their backers can gain ground during the 14th NATO Workshop, a forum of security and political issues which began Saturday in Prague.
But the highest U.S. official attending the Prague conference will be Deputy Secretary of Defence John White.

French President Jacques Chirac pressed his case for Romania's acceptance in the first wave during a meeting on Saturday with Clinton at the Group of Seven summit in Denver, but Clinton aides said the U.S. would not budge.
The alliance operates by consensus and the three U.S. choices appear to be the only ones which all 16 members would support, so a larger expansion appears unlikely this time.

Washington says possible NATO membership should remain indefinitely open to any European country not selected in Madrid, and much of the talk in Prague will be about what happens after the first round.

The four-day Prague forum will focus on Romanian President Emil Constantinescu's appearance Monday, where he is expected to make a final appeal for early membership, but also lay the groundwork for a quick second round should the invitation not come in Madrid.

Havel -- who backs any European country joining NATO if it fulfils basic criteria on democracy, human rights and an open economy -- said leaders still needed to convince citizens in Europe and the U.S. of the continued need for the alliance.

Opinion polls show that still fewer than half of Czechs want the country to join NATO, the lowest support among the three top aspirants, even though NATO membership has been a top post-Communist priority of the Prague government.

"It is very important to explain to our citizens, especially to those who still have their doubts, that unfortunately, defence is important, because unfortunately, there are still threats to human freedom," Havel said.
